Agua Caliente means hot water, and Native people used and considered these springs sacred long before anyone else showed up. Quiz: in 1895, a Captain Boyes drilled down just 70 feet. What did he hit? [[pause 4]] 112-degree hot water! He built a resort hotel, which burned down in a wildfire in 1923. Its replacement became the Sonoma Mission Inn. And in World War Two, the Navy borrowed it as a rest centre for sailors and Marines back from the Pacific, including those Guadalcanal veterans. From one of the worst battles in history, straight to soft beds and cherry pie.

This one's a darker story, but an important one. Off to the west, near the village of Eldridge, are the grounds of the Sonoma Developmental Center, which for over a century was a big state institution for people with developmental disabilities. It opened here in 1891. California passed a forced sterilisation law in 1909, only the third state to do so. From 1918, the superintendent here, F. O. Butler, was a big believer in it, and personally performed at least a thousand operations. The centre even admitted people just to sterilise them and send them home. It was said to have sterilised more people than any other institution in the world, and risky medical experiments on residents went on into the 1960s. It finally closed at the end of 2018. Not every story on a road trip is a happy one, but this one's worth knowing.

Up on the slopes of Sonoma Mountain, above the village of Glen Ellen, is the ranch of Jack London, and his life was as wild as his books. Born in San Francisco in 1876, he was an oyster pirate in the bay as a teenager, sailed off to the Klondike gold rush at 21, and came back a committed socialist. Quiz: in 1903 he sold The Call of the Wild, one of the most famous books ever, to a magazine. How much do you think he got for it? [[pause 5]] 750 dollars! In 1905 he bought an abandoned winery here and called it Beauty Ranch. Then he started building his dream house, Wolf House: 26 rooms, nine fireplaces, built of massive stone to survive earthquakes, with fancy new stuff like electric lights, refrigeration and even a built-in vacuum cleaner. He and his wife Charmian spent over 80,000 dollars on it. And then, on the 22nd of August 1913, just before they were due to move in, it burned down. He was devastated, deep in debt, and he died at the ranch in 1916, aged just forty. His ashes are under a rock from the ruins of Wolf House. He also wrote a novel called The Valley of the Moon, a translation of the Native name for the Sonoma Valley. You can still walk to the stone ruins today.

Here's something you could find in the gravel around here: natural volcanic glass! The geology maps around Glen Ellen and Kenwood show a layer called the Glen Ellen Formation: river gravel made mostly of eroded volcanic rock, famous for its pebbles of obsidian. Up in the hills there's a lava called the Rhyolite of Adobe Canyon, glassy and grey-white with swirly folded bands, about 5.3 million years old. Nearby Anna-dell State Park's whole history is written in this rock: Native Americans used its obsidian, and then, quiz, in the early 1900s people quarried its volcanic rock for something you've definitely walked on. What? [[pause 5]] Cobblestones! And some biologists say Anna-dell has the best untouched oak woodland anywhere.

This next town tried on more names than a teenager tries on outfits. Kenwood sits on an old Mexican ranch called Los Gee-lee-kose, granted in 1837 to a Scottish sea captain who never even lived on it. In 1850 he sold it to another Scot, William Hood, a cabinet-maker who'd climbed the mountain above the valley, fallen in love with the view, and made his fortune building houses in Gold Rush San Francisco to afford it. The mountain's now called Hood Mountain. When the railroad arrived in 1887, the town tried Rohrerville, then Los Gee-lee-kose, then South Los Gee-lee-kose. Quiz: why do you think people wanted to change it again? [[pause 4]] Nobody could pronounce Gee-lee-kose! So around 1895 they voted for Kenwood. Either because settlers came from Kenwood in Illinois, or because English families knew Kenwood House in London. Maybe both! Up to the north-east is Sugarloaf Ridge State Park. When the state planned to close it in 2011 to save money, a group of volunteers called Team Sugarloaf took it over and reopened it. They even run an observatory up there.

Welcome to Santa Rosa, the biggest city in California's wine country! And it has a creek with a pretty grim name. Let me explain. Before Europeans arrived, the Santa Rosa plain belonged to a powerful Poe-moe group called the Bitakomtara. They controlled it tightly: outsiders needed permission to pass through, and if they didn't ask, the penalties were harsh. They gathered for ceremonies on Santa Rosa Creek, near today's Spring Lake. Colonisation brought violence, enslavement and smallpox, and devastated them, though their descendants still live in the region. The first European home here was built in the 1830s by María López de Carrillo, a widow from San Diego, whose daughter had married General Vuh-lay-oh. Quiz: before she arrived, settlers from Sonoma used to slaughter cattle where two creeks meet, and one creek got named after it. Matanza means what in Spanish? [[pause 4]] Slaughter! So that's Matanzas Creek. Lovely. In the 1850s her son helped lay out the downtown grid around a central square, and the city still follows it.

Near downtown Santa Rosa is the house and garden of Luther Burbank, one of the most famous plant breeders who ever lived. And Julia, Adam, there's a really good chance you've eaten his work. He was born in Massachusetts in 1849, the thirteenth of fifteen kids. As a young man he bred a new potato, sold the rights for 150 dollars, and used the money to move to Santa Rosa in 1875. Inspired by Charles Darwin, he crossed plants on an enormous scale and created more than 800 varieties: the Shasta daisy, the Santa Rosa plum, a white blackberry, a spineless cactus for cattle. Quiz: a natural variant of his potato became the most widely grown potato in the United States. And a big share of one very famous fast-food chain's french fries are made from it. Which chain? [[pause 5]] McDonald's! The Russet Burbank is the classic french fry potato. So next time you have McDonald's fries, say thanks to Luther. He's buried in his garden here, under a cedar tree.

Okay, Peanuts fans! Santa Rosa was home to Charles Schulz, the creator of Charlie Brown and Snoopy. He grew up in Minnesota, the son of a barber, loved ice hockey, and moved out here in 1958. He kept drawing Peanuts right up until he died in 2000. In 1969 he and his wife built an ice rink here, and everyone calls it Snoopy's Home Ice. Quiz: what do you think the café inside the rink is called? [[pause 5]] The Warm Puppy! Every summer it hosts Snoopy's Senior World Hockey Tournament for older players from around the world. Down the street is the Charles M. Schulz Museum, with a 22-foot mural made of 3,588 Peanuts comic strips that together make a picture of Lucy holding the football for Charlie Brown. And here's my favourite Santa Rosa coincidence. Schulz's very first published drawing, in 1937, was of his family dog Spike, who ate pins, tacks and razor blades. He sent it to Ripley's Believe It or Not, and they ran it! And Robert Ripley, who created Believe It or Not? Born right here in Santa Rosa.

Believe it or not, Robert Ripley was born right here in Santa Rosa, in 1890. He left high school after his dad died, started drawing sports cartoons for newspapers at sixteen, and moved to New York in 1913. In 1918 he drew his very first Believe It or Not cartoon, all about weird facts and feats, and readers loved it. They started mailing him their own oddities: funny-shaped vegetables, strangely marked pets, you name it. He took his facts seriously enough to hire a full-time researcher. And by 1929 the panel was running in 360 newspapers in 17 languages, followed by radio and TV shows. Quiz: Ripley also held a sports title. Which sport? [[pause 5]] Handball! He was New York State handball champion in 1926. Believe it or not. A perfect Santa Rosan for a day full of oddities.

Okay, a little earthquake talk. Somewhere under this part of Santa Rosa runs one of the most dangerous faults in the Bay Area. You've probably heard of the Hayward Fault, under Berkeley and Oakland. Well, this side of the bay has its partner: the Rodgers Creek Fault, running right through Santa Rosa. In 2016 scientists showed the two are actually connected under San Pablo Bay, making one fault about 120 miles long, from north of Heldz-burg all the way to San Jose. It's the kind of fault where the ground on the other side slides sideways, to your right. Quiz: on the evening of the 1st of October 1969, Santa Rosa got hit by not one, but how many earthquakes, about an hour and twenty minutes apart? [[pause 4]] Two! Magnitude 5.6 and 5.7. Chimneys fell, sidewalks buckled, pipes burst, and one person died. The damage was worse than expected, and modelling suggests the city sits where a basin full of sediment amplifies the shaking. Luckily it was evening, so few people were on the streets. Afterwards the city started earthquake-proofing its old brick buildings.

Over the hill from Calistoga, Highway 128 drops into Knights Valley, a small, quiet valley with the warmest climate in Sonoma County. In 1843 the Mexican governor rewarded a soldier from the Sonoma garrison, José de los Santos Berreyesa, with almost 18,000 acres, which included this valley and even the hot springs at Calistoga. Quiz: what do you think he used this beautiful valley for? [[pause 4]] His own private hunting preserve! And the adobe hunting lodge he built is still standing. The English name comes from Thomas Knight, a guy from Maine who'd been one of the Bear Flag rebels in Sonoma in 1846. He bought a big chunk of the ranch, and his name stuck.

Chalk Hill has a secret: there's no chalk. The hills to the south-west are the Chalk Hill wine area, named after one prominent hill. Quiz: so what's the white stuff in the soil really? [[pause 4]] Volcanic ash! White tuff, from the eruptions of the Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh area, the same volcanism that turned the Petrified Forest to stone. It's said to be great for white grapes, and there's a warm band of air here, so harvest often comes in September, weeks before the neighbours. A bit further on, along Alexander Valley Road, the maps show a basalt lava flow and that obsidian-studded Glen Ellen gravel again. These are some of the last outposts of the big volcanic field, before the land turns to the old sea-floor rocks closer to the coast.

You're entering the Alexander Valley, the big, vine-filled valley of the Russian River north of Heldz-burg. It's the largest and most fully planted wine region in Sonoma County, with more than a hundred wineries. The story starts with a ranch called Sotoyome, almost 49,000 acres, named after a Wah-po group. It went to Henry Fitch, a San Diego sea captain who was General Vuh-lay-oh's brother-in-law. Fitch never lived here. He hired a manager, Cyrus Alexander, with a deal that after four years, Alexander would get a chunk of land and some cattle. Alexander settled down, and the valley took his name, even though the American land commission later rejected his claim to it. Ouch. Quiz: Alexander's replacement as ranch manager was the brother of a very famous Wild West frontiersman. Who? [[pause 5]] Kit Carson! His brother Mose Carson ran the ranch after 1845. And a wine note: Jordan winery here, with its French-style château from 1976, had a long-time winemaker who was trained by André Chelly-stcheff, the Bowl-you legend from Rutherford.

Heldz-burg is named after a squatter, and it gave the world lemon pepper. Seriously. It sits on the Russian River where three famous wine regions meet: the Alexander Valley, the Dry Creek Valley and the Russian River Valley. The Poe-moe built villages along the river here. The name comes from Harmon Heald, an Ohio businessman who squatted on the land from 1850, then bought a piece of it in 1857 when the owners auctioned off land to pay their taxes. The railroad arrived in 1872. And when Prohibition shut the wineries of Dry Creek Valley, which had been one of California's top Zinfandel regions, a lot of the land was switched to plums and prunes. Quiz: what famous seasoning was first developed commercially here in 1967? It's in the title. [[pause 3]] Lemon pepper! Thanks, Heldz-burg. If you cross the old steel bridge into town, that's the Heldz-burg Memorial Bridge from 1921, one of only thirteen bridges of its design in the whole country. People have been crossing the river at this exact spot since the 1850s, and the beach next to it is still a favourite swimming spot.

Here's a strong woman for you: Isabelle Simi. Simi Winery was started in San Francisco in 1876 by two Italian brothers who'd come for the Gold Rush, and they moved it here in 1881, paying 2,250 dollars in gold coins. From 1904, Giuseppe Simi's daughter Isabelle ran it, and she kept making wine right through Prohibition, storing it in the stone cellars. So when Prohibition ended in 1933, Simi was one of the only wineries with wine ready to sell. Clever. And in 1973 Simi hired Maryann Graf, the first woman to graduate from an American university with a degree in winemaking. Just north of town, Lytton has had a wild run: a luxury resort in 1872, then a boys' military school, a sanitarium, and for decades an orphanage. In 2017, the Lytton Band of Poe-moe Indians bought it back for around 30 million dollars, after years of trying to recover land they'd lost.

Quiz: the town of Windsor, coming up, got its name from a Pony Express rider. Why do you think he chose Windsor? [[pause 4]] He thought the countryside looked like the grounds of Windsor Castle, back in his home country of England! He was Hiram Lewis, the first postmaster, in 1855. Long before that, it was a Southern Poe-moe village called Tsoliikawai, which means blackbird field. Windsor had a rough start to the 1900s: a fire wiped out the town centre in 1905, then the 1906 earthquake damaged buildings that were still being repaired. In World War Two, the army built an air base on the south side of town, now the Charles M. Schulz airport. And in 1943 there was even a camp here for German prisoners of war.

Westside Road is one of the prettiest drives in wine country, winding along the river through some of the most celebrated Pinot Noir country in California. Cool, foggy, gorgeous. But check out the rocks too. The geology maps show this road crossing old sea-floor sandstone that got dragged down into the Earth in a subduction zone, squeezed at huge pressure, and turned blue with a mineral called glaucophane, then somehow made it back to the surface. It's called blueschist, and it's rare all over the world. Quiz: why do you think it's so rare? [[pause 5]] Because it can only form deep in a subduction zone, and then it has to find its way all the way back up to the surface. Further along you'll pass may-lahnj, that fruitcake rock, and old river gravels on flat benches cut into the bedrock. So on this lovely, winding road, you're driving over bits of an ancient ocean floor that went down into the Earth and came back up.

Welcome to Sebastopol, which has one of the best name stories on the map. Quiz: the town was originally called Pine Grove. Then in the late 1850s, a bar fight broke out. And somehow that led to the new name. How? [[pause 6]] A bystander said the long, drawn-out brawl was like the siege of Sevastopol, a Russian port in the Crimean War. And the name stuck! Remember Yount-vill? It was going to be called Sebastopol too, but this town got there first. The Coast Mee-wok and Poe-moe were here first, and the town sits on top of several of their village sites. Later there was a busy Chinatown downtown from the 1880s. Then came the apples. Sebastopol called itself the Grah-ven-steen Apple Capital of the World. The Grah-ven-steen is an old Danish apple, from the 1600s or earlier: tart, juicy, perfect for apple sauce and cider, but it doesn't keep, so you can only get it in season. There's still a Grah-ven-steen Apple Fair every August. These days the old apple warehouses have turned into The Barlow, full of tasting rooms and restaurants.

Luther Burbank, our potato guy, needed more space than his Santa Rosa garden, so in 1885 he bought a farm here in the Gold Ridge area. Quiz: at its peak, how many plant experiments do you think he had going on this farm at once? [[pause 5]] Over 60,000, by some estimates! Three acres of it survive, with more than 250 of his plants, looked after entirely by volunteers. And Sebastopol used to have electric trolleys! From 1903 to 1947, the Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railway ran around the county, partly to break the big railroad's monopoly. All that's left is one passenger car in a museum, and its old stone power house on Petaluma Avenue, which has, very fittingly, been turned into a series of brew pubs.

Here's a surprise for a town twenty miles from the ocean. The geology maps show that Highway 116 north of Sebastopol runs for more than ten kilometres across an old sea floor! It's called the Wilson Grove Formation: pale sandstone laid down in the sea between about eleven and three million years ago, and in places it's full of broken-up seashells. So all this gentle Gold Ridge country around Sebastopol used to be under the ocean, and got lifted up as the Coast Ranges rose. To the east, the Santa Rosa plain is made of gravel washed out of the hills. And as we head north toward the river, the road crosses into much older, harder rock from that geological junk drawer, the Franciscan Complex.

Grayton, just off the highway, is a little apple town that turned into a wine town. And quiz: it was once at the very edge of an empire. Which one? [[pause 5]] The Russian Empire! Grayton is about as far south and east as Russian colonisation in the Americas ever reached. The Russians at Fort Ross on the coast needed food, so in 1836 their farm expert, Yegor Chernykh, set up a farm between here and Occidental, with barracks, vegetables, wheat, and a big vineyard. So Russians helped plant some of the first vines around here! There's a sadder story in these hills too. In 1851, many California tribes signed treaties promising them land, but the U.S. never ratified them. In 1920 the government bought fifteen acres near here for the homeless Coast Mee-wok and Poe-moe people of the area. When seventy-five people tried to move in, they found only three acres were livable. And in 1958, the government ended the rancheria altogether.

Freestone, population about thirty-two, is the gateway to the Bo-hee-mee-un Highway. It's named after a sandstone quarry, and it was the first historic district Sonoma County ever named, in 1974. And it has my favourite crime story of the trip. In 1876, a farmer built the Hinds Hotel here when he heard the railroad was coming, and the carpenters building the railway line stayed there. Quiz: according to first-hand reports, the innkeeper came up with a sneaky plan to keep his guests around longer. What did he do? [[pause 6]] He had parts of the bridge they were building secretly burned at night, so the job would take longer! He went to jail for it. Customer retention, Wild West style. And in the 1970s, the old hotel was the party headquarters for the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude while they built their famous Running Fence.

This next town has a creek named after a sailor who jumped ship, and a commune that tried to give its land to God. Welcome to Occidental! It was founded in 1876 as a stop on a railroad from the Saw-suh-lee-toe ferry up to the redwoods. A local landowner, a Danish sailor known as Dutch Bill Howard, who'd jumped ship in San Francisco Bay in 1849, gave the railroad its right-of-way. In return he got a free lifetime train pass, and the station was named after him. The creek next to the road is still Dutch Bill Creek. The railroad started a timber boom, and by 1877 there were six sawmills here. Then, a hundred years later: hippies! In 1966 Lou Gottlieb, from the folk band the Limeliters, bought land near here, and in 1967 he opened it to anyone who wanted to live there. Morning Star Ranch drew hundreds of people from San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury, and the county answered with arrests and bulldozers. Quiz: in 1969, Gottlieb tried to transfer the land to a new owner, to get the county off his back. Who? [[pause 5]] God! He deeded the land to God. The courts did not accept God as the owner.

Quiz: how much would you pay for a plot of land twenty-five feet by twelve, with a one-room cabin on it? [[pause 4]] In 1898, right here, it cost seventy-five dollars. This is Camp Meeker, named after Melvin Cyrus Meeker, a lumber baron who opened mills here around 1866. These redwoods built San Francisco, and then, after 1906, rebuilt it. Meeker is the same guy who sold the Bo-hee-mee-un Grove land to the Bo-hee-mee-un Club. Once the trees were cut down, he chopped the land into those tiny lots and sold them to San Franciscans wanting a summer escape. Now it's a little village of about 425 people tucked among the new redwoods, with some roads so steep and narrow they feel like old railway tracks. And the creek has become a happy conservation story: wild coho salmon came back to spawn in 2001, young salmon have been released here since 2006, and in 2009 an old swimming-hole dam, one of the worst salmon blockers in the whole watershed, was swapped for a footbridge.

The land from the Golden Gate up to the Sonoma coast, and east to Sonoma Creek, was home to the Coast Mee-wok. That includes the hills around Sebastopol and Freestone and the lower Sonoma Valley. They lived in small bands with no central government. In spring they headed to the coast for salmon, shellfish and seaweed. The rest of the year, acorns were the staple, plus deer and rabbit. Quiz: Coast Mee-wok hunters had a clever trick for sneaking up on deer. What do you think they did? [[pause 5]] They rubbed themselves with a plant called Brewer's angelica to hide their scent! They also drank yerba buena tea as medicine, made tattoo ink from burned poison oak, and built cone-shaped houses called kotcha from tule reeds or redwood bark. Amazing basket makers too. The word Mee-wok just means people. Within a couple of generations of the Spanish arriving, the people of this region lost their land and were devastated by disease. Later, broken federal treaties left them landless. If you ever visit Point Reyes, there's a recreated Coast Mee-wok village there called Koo-lay Lock-low.

You're on the Silverado Trail, the quieter road up the east side of the Napa Valley, 29 miles long. And quiz: back in the 1880s, travellers on this road had to watch out for a famous someone. Who? [[pause 4]] A stagecoach robber called Black Bart! He preyed on travellers here. Things got safer when a motor bus service started in 1910. The road started in 1852 as a trail used when floods made the main valley road impassable. Later it became the wagon road for the mercury mines on Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh, and the first permanent road between Napa and Calistoga. Silver was found in the valley in 1858. Today there are at least forty wineries along it, and every March it hosts the Napa Valley Marathon. The hills just east of Napa are called Coombsville, after Nathan Coombs, the guy who founded Napa. Volcanic soil, and fog that rolls in early and hangs around late.

Okay, wine fans, sit up! You're about to pass the vineyard that beat the French. This is the Stags Leap District, a tiny pocket of land only about one mile by three, with hills on three sides. Here's the story. Warren Win-ee-ar-ski fell in love with wine while spending a year in Italy studying Machiavelli. He moved his family to Napa in 1968 and worked at Robert Mon-dah-vee's new winery. Then he tasted a homemade wine from a neighbour, Nathan Fay, and thought, this is it. In 1970 he bought the 44 acres next door. Quiz: what was growing on the land when he bought it? [[pause 5]] Prunes, cherries and walnuts! He ripped them out and planted Cabernet. And his 1973 Cabernet went to Paris in 1976 and took first place, beating Château Mouton-Rothschild and Haut-Brion. The magazine Decanter called it a victory that put California on the winemaking map. And the soil here is special: clay from the Napa River mixed with volcanic stuff washed down from the Vacka Mountains.

Two wineries along here tell two sides of the Napa story. First, Frog's Leap, started in 1981 by a doctor and a winemaker at a spot known as Frog Farm. Quiz: the winemaker got his start at a very famous winery nearby. Can you guess which, from the name? [[pause 4]] Stag's Leap! Frog Farm plus Stag's Leap equals Frog's Leap. And the corks say Ribbit. But behind the jokes, it's serious stuff: it was the first Napa winery to use certified organic grapes, the vines aren't irrigated, and since 2005 solar panels supply most of its power. Then Heitz Cellar, from 1961, back when Napa had only about two dozen wineries left. Joe Heitz, a farm boy from Illinois, was one of the first seven people ever to graduate from UC Davis in winemaking, in 1951. He trained under the legendary Chelly-stcheff, bought a little vineyard for 5,000 dollars, and his Martha's Vineyard Cabernet became a Napa legend. It was even one of the reds tasted in Paris in 1976.

Look east around Saint Huh-lee-nuh. That forested ridge is Howell Mountain. And here's a surprise: Napa was winning medals in Paris long before 1976! Two French winemakers set up there in 1877, and Charles Krug planted about a hundred acres by 1884. Then a man called W. S. Keyes planted his vineyard in 1880. Quiz: at the Paris Exposition of 1899, what did his wines win? [[pause 4]] Gold and bronze medals! And in 1904, his claret won the grand prize at the St. Louis World's Fair. So 1976 wasn't the first time Napa impressed the French. It was just the most famous.

Mark Twain and Clark Gable both came to soak in springs near here. Near Saint Huh-lee-nuh was White Sulphur Springs, said to be the oldest warm-spring resort in Northern California, opened in 1852. Native people used the springs long before that. In the late 1800s, rich San Franciscans got here by steamboat, then train, then stagecoach. Quiz: at its peak, how many guests could the grand hotel hold? [[pause 4]] A thousand! After the 1906 earthquake it housed refugees. Sadly, fire was always its enemy: three grand hotels burned over the years, and the 2020 Glass Fire destroyed most of what was left.

You're climbing Spring Mountain Road into the My-uh-kah-muss. Quiz: where's the actual Spring Mountain? [[pause 4]] Trick question! There isn't one. Spring Mountain was the name for a whole green, well-watered area of hills full of springs and little streams, not one peak. It was one of the first places in Napa recognised for grapes. The first documented vineyard was Charles Lemme's La Perla, planted in 1874, and in the 1880s the Beringer brothers planted up here too. The vineyards are on steep slopes, so the crops are small: it makes less than two percent of Napa's wine. Up over the county line, the road becomes Saint Huh-lee-nuh Road and drops down toward the start of Mark West Creek.

You're crossing a mountain range that the federal government couldn't decide how to spell! These are the My-uh-kah-muss Mountains, 52 miles long, separating the Napa and Sonoma valleys. The highest point is Cobb Mountain, 4,724 feet, and the rain that falls up here ends up in Pew-tah Creek, Sonoma Creek, Santa Rosa Creek and Mark West Creek. The name probably comes from a Wah-po village called Maiya'kma, near Calistoga. Quiz: the federal naming board made one decision on the spelling, then reversed it in 1941. Which spelling did they finally pick? [[pause 5]] Mayacmas! Without the second a. And plenty of people still write My-uh-kah-muss. And there's still a creek called Mah-kah-muh. So, honestly, spell it however you like. The road you're on crosses a volcanic landscape: white pumice from an eruption about 4.84 million years ago, grey lava from about 7.9 million, and swirly glassy lava from about 5.3 million. And about ten million years ago, these mountains were probably covered in cypress forest.

Two wineries went to war with the federal government over one word: Calistoga! Here's the deal. Official wine regions are created by the federal government, and once one exists, wineries have to use mostly grapes from that area to put its name on the label. In 2003, Bo Barrett of Chateau Monteh-lay-nuh asked for a Calistoga wine region. But two wineries, Calistoga Cellars and Calistoga Estate, already had Calistoga in their brand names. Quiz: what do you think they'd have to do if the region was approved? [[pause 5]] Either use at least 85 percent Calistoga grapes, or change their names! They fought it hard. It finally got approved in 2009, and they got three years to comply. Next door, Diamond Mountain had a fight over one word too, and the owners of a winery with that trademark won, so it's officially the Diamond Mountain District. And in Sonoma, a giant region called Northern Sonoma was created in 1985 largely because of the huge Gallo winery.

Okay, let's talk about the event that made Sacramento, and, honestly, most of what you'll see today. On the 24th of January 1848, James Marshall was building a sawmill for the pioneer John Sutter, up the American River, when he spotted something shiny in the water. Gold! Sutter tried to keep it secret, because he was worried a rush would wreck his plans for a farming empire. Quiz: who do you think spread the news anyway? Hint: you've already met him today. [[pause 5]] Sam Brannan! And about 300,000 people poured into California. San Francisco went from about 200 people in 1846 to around 36,000 by 1852, and California became a state in 1850. The Gold Rush echoes through this whole trip. West Sacramento was a rest stop for miners. Dixon started as a halfway stop for them. Alfred Tubbs made his fortune selling rope to the rush, then founded Chateau Monteh-lay-nuh. Dr. Bale of the grist mill went off mining and died of a fever. And all those new people were thirsty, so vineyards spread across Napa and Sonoma in the 1850s. But it was a catastrophe for Native Californians. Disease, hunger and violence made their populations collapse, and whole tribes were driven from their land, including the Pat-win of this valley.

South of the freeway, out of sight, is one of the most important places in California: the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta. The Yo-lo Bypass floods drain into it, and so does about half of all the water that runs off California's land. Here's how it formed. Around 560,000 years ago, water broke through the coastal mountains and carved the Car-keen-ess Strait and San Francisco Bay. All the rivers had to squeeze out through that one narrow gap, which slowed them down. The tides pushed back up and slowed them even more, so the rivers dropped their mud and built a huge freshwater marsh full of channels and peat islands. Then people drained it. Today there are about 57 reclaimed islands, ringed by 1,100 miles of levees. Quiz: when you drain peat soil, something weird happens to the land. What? [[pause 5]] It sinks! The peat breaks down and blows away, so a lot of the Delta now sits below sea level, behind its levees. That's why it's nicknamed California's Holland. And giant pumps at the south end send Delta water to farms and to the cities of Southern California. So pretty much every California water fight ends up here.

Here's a handy one if you ever drive this valley in winter. From November to March, after the first big rains, the Central Valley gets something called tule fog, named after the tule reeds that used to cover the wetlands. On long, still winter nights, the damp ground cools fast, and the cold air near the ground gets trapped under warmer air above, until it turns into a thick, low blanket of fog. It can stretch over 400 miles, from Bakersfield to Red Bluff. Quiz: in 2005, tule fog was the number one cause of what in California? [[pause 4]] Weather-related car accidents! So if you ever see this valley disappear into a white wall on a winter morning, slow way down. Today, in late October, we're just ahead of the season. Phew.

Every vineyard and orchard you pass depends on people who rarely show up in the wine brochures. Here's their story. The first workers were Native Californians, often forced. The Pat-win were made to work for free on ranches and in mines, and by 1870 only a few Native people remained in the Napa Valley, working as labourers and servants. In the late 1800s, Chinese and Japanese immigrants worked Vacka-vill's orchards. In World War Two there was even a camp of German prisoners of war near Windsor, put to work. The biggest change was the Bracero Program, a deal between the U.S. and Mexico that started in Stockton in August 1942 to fill wartime labour shortages. Over 22 years, it offered millions of contracts to Mexican workers. Quiz: what minimum hourly wage were they promised? [[pause 4]] Thirty cents an hour. The programme ended in 1964, and economists later found that ending it pushed farms toward machines. Today, around a third of Napa County's people are Hispanic or Latino. And the tension between luxury and labour is very much alive: in 2026, Thomas Keller of the French Laundry opposed a plan for 120 apartments in Yount-vill for workers who'd been priced out of town.

Have you noticed something about the Napa Valley floor? There are basically no housing developments or shopping malls between the towns. That's not luck. It's one of the most important land decisions in California history. Neighbouring counties let big stretches of farmland turn into houses and shops. But in 1968, Napa's winemakers and civic leaders went the other way. Using a new state law that gave tax breaks for keeping land in farming, they created an agricultural preserve on the valley floor. Quiz: was Napa the first county in California to do this? [[pause 4]] Yes! It was the first one in the state. It started at 23,000 acres and grew to over 30,000. Then in 1990, voters went further and froze county zoning changes for thirty years, unless two-thirds of voters agreed. The fights never stop. Locals battled the Wine Train in the eighties. County rules even stop Castello dee Amo-roza from hosting weddings. And now the big fight is about whether the people who work here can afford to live here. The preserve kept the valley green. Who gets to live in it is the next argument.

Wine isn't the only crop around here with a complicated legal history. California has been at the front of cannabis politics for half a century. In 1972, it held the first ballot vote in the nation to legalise cannabis. Quiz: did it pass? [[pause 4]] Nope! It failed. But in 1996, California became the first state to legalise medical cannabis, and in 2016, voters legalised recreational use, with 57 percent of the vote. Legalisation turned out to be messy. Growers had to register and get permits, and more than half of the medical dispensaries closed. Legal businesses pay hefty taxes, while illegal growers keep going in remote rural areas. And it's all still illegal under federal law. So, a bit like the winemakers during Prohibition, today's cannabis farmers live in a weird legal twilight zone between what the state allows and what Washington forbids.

We've met Russians again and again today: a river, a mountain, a farm near Grayton. So here's the whole story. Russian traders pushed east across Siberia and the North Pacific, and in 1799 they set up a colony in Alaska. Their business was fur, especially sea otters. From 1803, American ship captains took Alaska Native hunters down the California coast to hunt otters, and between 1805 and 1812 alone they gathered over 22,000 pelts. In 1812 the Russians built their own base, Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, in the land of the Kuh-shy-uh Poe-moe. It was super diverse: Native Californians, Native Alaskans, Russians, Finns and Swedes, all together. They explored the river and planted a farm and vineyard near Grayton. And the Spanish and Mexicans got so nervous that they built the mission at Sonoma partly to block them. Quiz: in 1841 the Russians decided to sell Fort Ross. They offered it to General Vuh-lay-oh, but the Mexican officials dithered. Who ended up buying it? [[pause 5]] John Sutter! The same Sutter on whose land gold was discovered seven years later. Small world.

Here's a wine story you won't hear in many tasting rooms. California's first wine grape was the Mission grape, brought by the Spanish, and it ruled until about 1880. Then the Gold Rush created thirsty customers, and Ah-go-stone Hair-uss-tee brought in cuttings from 165 of Europe's best vineyards. Charles Krug, a Prussian political dissident, learned winemaking from Hair-uss-tee before starting his own winery in Saint Huh-lee-nuh. And north of Santa Rosa, at the utopian colony of Fountain Grove, the vineyards were run by Nagasawa Kanaye. Quiz: what nickname do you think he earned? [[pause 4]] The Grape King of California! He was one of the biggest winemakers in the state, and he threw lavish dinners for guests like John Muir, Thomas Edison and Henry Ford. And according to the history books, Fountain Grove's cellars kept flowing right through Prohibition. Wink. It's a reminder that wine country's history is a lot more diverse than the fancy châteaux suggest: Spanish missionaries, a Hungarian adventurer, German and Italian immigrants, a Finnish sea captain, and a Grape King, all on land that was Poe-moe, Wah-po, Mee-wok and Pat-win for thousands of years.

Good morning, road-trippers! Day two. Mike's on driving duty, Adam and Julia are in charge of snacks, and I'm in charge of the chat. Here's the plan. We follow the Russian River to the ocean, then drive down the wild Sonoma Coast to Bo-day-guh Bay, where Hitchcock made birds terrifying. Then either along Toe-mah-less Bay and Point Reyes, or inland through Petaluma, to the giant redwoods of Muir Woods. And finally over the Golden Gate Bridge, through San Francisco, to the airport. Big trees first, if you've got an hour before you leave: Armstrong Redwoods is just north of Gurn-vill. The Parson Jones Tree, a hundred yards from the entrance, is more than 310 feet tall, and the Colonel Armstrong Tree is over 1,400 years old. And Muir Woods is later today. Seafood too: oysters on Toe-mah-less Bay, and crab country around Bo-day-guh Bay. I've packed the rest of today with a bit of everything. Earthquakes and geography, obviously, because we'll be driving along the San Andreas Fault for a good chunk of the morning. A nuclear power fight that Julia will enjoy. Offshore wind politics for Adam. Some infrastructure and logistics stories for Mike. A famous sailing comeback, the Olympics that came out of nowhere, and a few things that happened in the news this past year or two. Let's go find the ocean.

Picture this road with a little narrow-gauge train chugging along beside the river. From the 1870s, the North Pacific Coast Railroad ran from Cah-zuh-dair-oh, through Mon-tee Ree-oh and Duncans Mills, all the way down to the ferry at Saw-suh-lee-toe. Remember that name, because the same railway also stopped at Valley Ford, Toe-mah-less, Marshall and Point Reyes Station. We're basically following its ghost all morning. The business model changed twice. First, it hauled redwood lumber to build San Francisco: in 1877 Alexander Duncan set up a sawmill right here, and a town grew around it, with two hotels, a saloon, a blacksmith and a livery stable. When the timber ran out, the railroad pivoted to tourists, carrying San Franciscans up to summer cabins. Mon-tee Ree-oh, back there, rebranded as Vacation Wonderland, complete with a seven-story hotel downtown, and parts of the 1942 Oscar-winning film Holiday Inn were shot at a resort there. By the 1930s the trains had stopped and Duncans Mills faded away. It was rescued in 1976 by a Bicentennial restoration project. There's still an original depot here, with some of the old railroad cars parked outside.

There it is! The Russian River meets the Pacific, right here at Jenner. Population: about a hundred and twenty. The town is named after Dr. Elijah Jenner, a dentist and inventor from Vermont who came west for the Gold Rush in 1850. While mining, he designed a pump that could lift water a hundred feet. Quiz: when he applied for the patent, he sent in a model of the pump. What was so special about it? [[pause 5]] It was made of pure gold! It's the only golden model the Patent Office has ever received. A proper Gold Rush flex. Now watch the river mouth. In summer, the waves build a sandbar right across it, and the river backs up into a lagoon until the water gets high enough, somewhere between four and a half and seven feet at the Jenner visitor center, and then it breaks through. In winter, the sheltered beach on the north side is where harbor seals have their pups.

Movie quiz! Down on the right is Goat Rock Beach, with that huge flat-topped rock barely hanging on to the land. In 1985, a very famous adventure movie about a group of kids hunting for pirate treasure filmed its ending on this beach. Which one? [[pause 5]] The Goonies! Goonies never say die. Those rocks out in the sea are called sea stacks. For about 170 million years, an ocean plate was diving under North America, scraping off pillow lava, chert and sandstone and crushing it all into a jumble called may-lahnj: hard blocks floating in softer, ground-up rock. The waves wash away the soft stuff and leave the hard blocks standing. Goat Rock is one big block of grey-wacky sandstone. And my favourite fact on this coast: about a mile south of the river there's a blue rock with rubbing marks two to four meters up. Far too high for cows. Scientists think mammoths used it as a back-scratcher, as recently as 40,000 years ago.

Quick-fire facts on the Sonoma Coast. One: it's seventeen miles of state beaches from just north of Jenner down to Bo-day-guh Head. Two: it's disappearing. Those soft bluffs lose one to three feet a year on average, more in a stormy winter. Three: it's also rising. You're driving on a flat shelf above the beach called a marine terrace. It's old sea floor, lifted up over the ages. Some sea stacks are even stranded up on the terrace, away from the water, because they started life on the sea floor before it rose. Four: people have lived here a very long time. Dozens of Coast Mee-wok and Poe-moe shell middens, basically ancient kitchen rubbish heaps, have been found along here. Five: keep an eye out to sea for gray whales, harbor seals and sea lions.

Here's a bit of infrastructure politics, Mike, since you're the one stuck behind the camper vans. Ever wondered why Highway 1 is just one lane each way, even on busy summer weekends? It's the law. The 1976 California Coastal Act specifically bans widening Highway 1 beyond one lane in each direction in the rural parts of the coastal zone. It's enforced by the California Coastal Commission, which has quasi-judicial control over development and public access along 1,100 miles of coastline. Its zone runs inland from about a thousand yards up to five miles. Inside it, almost anything, from a new house to splitting a plot of land or changing how people get to the beach, needs a coastal permit. It's one of the most powerful land-use bodies in America, and it's in constant fights. In 2019, for example, it allowed a seawall to protect apartments built in 1972, but refused one for townhomes built in 1984, because the Act only protects buildings that existed when it was passed. The townhome owners sued. Debate for the car: is this brilliant protection of the coast, or a planning system gone too far? You've got until Bo-day-guh Bay.

Welcome to Bo-day-guh Bay! Fishing boats, salty air, and a harbor tucked behind that long headland. It's named after Juan Francisco de la Bo-day-guh y Kwah-druh, a Spanish naval officer who sailed in here in 1775. In 1793 the Spanish parked a little garrison here with four cannons, because they'd heard the English might turn up. They didn't, so the guns went home to Monterey. Then the Russians turned up instead! In 1809 they put up the first Russian buildings in California here, before building Fort Ross, and called the place Port Room-yahnt-sev. Hollywood loves it too: The Birds, The Fog, I Know What You Did Last Summer, The Russians Are Coming. Quiz: in 2021, a famous American TV comedy needed to film a season in Ireland, but COVID made that impossible, so Bo-day-guh Bay played Ireland. Which show? [[pause 5]] It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia! A Californian fishing village pretending to be Ireland. With this fog, it works.

Lunch briefing, since I hear seafood is today's top priority. Crab first. The working boats in Bo-day-guh Bay, coming up, go after Dungeness crab, one of the most important seafood catches on the whole West Coast, found from Alaska's Aleutian Islands down to near Santa Barbara. The fishery was started by San Francisco fishermen back in 1848, the year gold was found. By the early 1900s, rules said you could only keep hard-shelled male crabs at least six inches across, and those are still the rules today. Most are caught in baited wire pots on a buoy, and every pot must be tied on with a biodegradable rot cord, so if it's lost it eventually opens and stops trapping crabs. Then oysters, on Toe-mah-less Bay, about forty minutes further on if you take the coast route. The two big farms, Hog Island and Toe-mah-less Bay Oyster Company, both sell to the public with picnic tables by the water, on the east shore near Marshall, right on Highway 1. Mike, as the operations man: oysters from bay to table in about fifty yards. Hard to beat that supply chain.

Story time. In August 1961, the people of Cap-ih-toe-luh, a seaside town further down this coast, woke up to something out of a nightmare. Thousands of seabirds were dive-bombing their houses, crashing into cars and dropping half-eaten fish on people's lawns. Alfred Hitchcock read about it. He was already working on a film based on a Daphne du Maurier story about birds attacking people, and he used the Cap-ih-toe-luh event as research. The result was The Birds, released in 1963 and set right here in Bo-day-guh Bay. Tippy Hed-ren, in her first film, drives up from San Francisco with a pair of lovebirds, and it goes very, very badly: gulls at the dock, crows at the schoolhouse, sparrows pouring down the chimney. Most of the birds were real. The gulls were caught at the San Francisco rubbish dump, and some of the crows were actually ravens. It took 370 special-effects shots, and the final shot was stitched together from 32 separate pieces. And what really happened in Cap-ih-toe-luh? Toxic algae had poisoned the birds. Nobody knew that in the 1960s. A darker footnote: decades later, Tippy Hed-ren said Hitchcock harassed her during filming. Today it's rated one of the greatest horror films ever made.

Julia, this one's for you. Across the harbor is Bo-day-guh Head, and it has a hole in it, literally. It's where America's anti-nuclear movement is said to have been born. In the late 1950s, the utility company PG&E planned to build a nuclear power plant on the headland, meant to be the first commercially viable one in the country. The fishermen worried about their livelihoods. A local landowner, Rose Gaffney, refused to sell, sued the company, and invited government officials to come and look at the fault lines on the site. In June 1963, protesters released 1,500 helium balloons, each carrying the message that it could represent a radioactive molecule of strontium 90 or iodine 131. The real clincher was geology. The San Andreas Fault runs right between Bo-day-guh Head and the mainland. The headland is on the Pacific Plate, the town's on the North American Plate, and in the 1906 earthquake the headland moved about fifteen feet. In 1964, after a negative review by the Atomic Energy Commission, PG&E gave up. By then they'd already dug the pit for the reactor. It filled with water, and the locals call it the Hole in the Head.

So where did California's nuclear story go next? Today it has exactly one working nuclear plant: Diablo Canyon, on the central coast, also run by PG&E. It makes about 8.6 percent of the state's electricity, and nearly a quarter of its carbon-free power. It was built less than a mile from a fault line nobody knew about at the time, and in 1981 nearly two thousand protesters were arrested there in just two weeks. In 2016, PG&E said it would close it in 2024 and 2025, partly because California's rules give renewables priority. Then the grid operators warned of blackouts, 79 scientists wrote an open letter, and in 2022 a new state law extended it to 2030. And Julia's world: fusion. At Livermore, on the other side of the Bay, the National Ignition Facility fires the world's most energetic laser at a tiny fuel capsule. On the 5th of December 2022 it got more energy out of the fuel than the laser put in: 3.15 megajoules out, from 2.05 in. The catch: making that laser pulse took about 300 megajoules from the grid. By 2025, shots had reached 8.6 megajoules. Julia, over to you: how far away is a fusion power plant?

This little village is Bo-day-guh, once called Bo-day-guh Corners, to tell it apart from the port down by the water. There were two Coast Mee-wok villages around here, and then in 1809 the Russians settled in the Salmon Creek valley. When the Russians left, around 1843, John Sutter bought their land, including this area. The sale included some hunting rights, a small boat, several rusty cannons and some old muskets. Bargain. The same year, a Captain Stephen Smith built the first lumber mill on the West Coast near here. The town proper began in 1853 with a saloon, a blacksmith and a hotel, which is the correct order of priorities. If the church and the schoolhouse look familiar, that's because they starred in The Birds. They're right here on the Bo-day-guh Highway, and the schoolhouse is where the crows gather on the climbing frame. And underfoot, the geology maps show the Wilson Grove Formation, sea-floor sandstone from the late My-oh-seen and Ply-oh-seen, very roughly ten to three million years ago. The same sandstone we met back in Sebastopol.

Adam, this one's yours. Out past Point Reyes is open Pacific, with some of the strongest offshore wind in the country. So where are all the turbines? The problem is depth. The seabed off California drops away fast, so instead of fixed turbines on the seabed like in the North Sea, it needs floating ones. In 2021 the Biden administration approved large areas off the coast for floating wind farms, and in 2022 California set a target of 25 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2045. Then, this year, in 2026, the second Trump administration negotiated a series of deals that stopped three of the state's five offshore wind projects. Meanwhile, on land, solar has boomed. By the end of 2023, solar was making 28 percent of California's electricity, the most of any state. And the law says 60 percent of the state's power must be renewable by 2030, and 100 percent by 2045. The headache is the duck curve. Solar floods the grid at midday, then disappears at sunset, just as everyone gets home, so other plants have to ramp up by about five gigawatts an hour. That's why solar with batteries is now worth so much more than solar without. Over to the analyst: would you rather back floating wind off this coast right now, or batteries?

Tiny Valley Ford, population about a hundred and fifty, in rolling dairy country. The Coast Mee-wok had a village here called Eh-wah-palt. There was a grain mill in the 1850s, and from 1876 the railway stopped here, so ranchers and fishers could ship their produce to San Francisco. Quiz: in 1976, the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude built a giant artwork that passed right through Valley Ford, running from Co-tah-tee all the way to Bo-day-guh Bay. What was it? [[pause 5]] A fence! Running Fence: a long white fabric fence over the hills and down into the ocean. Two more. Guitarists, take note: Shubb, the company that makes guitar capos, has its headquarters right here. And a grimmer one: run-off from the dairies has put so much nitrate in the groundwater that in 2017 the state warned pregnant women and babies not to drink the town's well water. Some restaurants truck their water in from Petaluma.

Welcome to Marin County, and to Toe-mah-less, population just under two hundred. The Coast Mee-wok had villages all around here, including one called Oo-too-mee-uh, near the town. The post office opened in 1854, spelled Tomalles, with two L's, and later lost one. And the North Pacific Coast Railroad came through in the 1870s. Toe-mah-less sits close to the San Andreas Fault, and you can still see the 1906 earthquake here, in the cemetery. One of the town's two cemeteries is older than the earthquake, and the damage to the old graves shows just how far the shaking reached.

That long, skinny bay is Toe-mah-less Bay: fifteen miles long, about a mile wide, and only eighteen feet deep on average. In 1603, Spanish explorers from the Viz-kuh-ee-no expedition saw it, assumed it was a river, and named it the Rio Grande de San Sebastián. But it's not a river. It's a fault. Toe-mah-less Bay is a drowned stretch of the San Andreas Fault. Everything on the far side, the Point Reyes Peninsula, is on the Pacific Plate. You're on the North American Plate. The fault runs from here down the Oh-lee-muh Valley to Buh-lee-nus Lagoon, and this road follows it nearly the whole way. The Coast Mee-wok had villages all around the bay. And the shells and clams from its shores weren't just food: they were used as money.

This stretch of shore is Marshall, and if anyone's hungry: oysters. The town is named after four Marshall brothers who started dairy farming here in the 1850s. There's still dairy, with the Straus Family Creamery based here, but the big business now is oysters and clams. The two biggest producers on Toe-mah-less Bay are Hog Island Oyster Company and Toe-mah-less Bay Oyster Company, and both sell straight to the public, with picnic tables right on this shore. If you stop, the local move is a bag of oysters at a table by the water. Mike, a supply-chain footnote. Just across the peninsula, the Drakes Bay Oyster Company farmed oysters inside the national seashore until the government refused to renew its permit in 2012. It fought all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court, which declined to hear the case in 2014, and the farm closed at the end of that year.

Welcome to Point Reyes Station, the little hub town for the Point Reyes peninsula. It started as the end of the railway line. When the trains arrived in 1875, it was called Oh-lee-muh Station. Then, in 1891 alone, the name changed three times: first to Marin, then back to Point Reyes, then finally Point Reyes Station. It used to be a real port on Toe-mah-less Bay, too. But cattle and European grasses caused erosion, and silt, small dams and landfill for farming raised the old salt marshes. Now the town is nearly a mile from the nearest tidal flats.

This crossroads is Oh-lee-muh, from a Coast Mee-wok name meaning coyote valley. For years people believed it was the epicenter of the 1906 earthquake, because the ground moved so much here. Scientists now think the epicenter was offshore, near Daly City. Now some very recent news. Those green hills inside Point Reyes National Seashore have been cattle ranches for well over a century, about 28,000 acres of dairy and beef, leased back to the ranchers when the park was created. But the ranches have been accused of polluting the creeks and Toe-mah-less Bay with E coli, and a 2022 inspection found raw sewage leaking from some of them. In January 2025, a deal brokered by The Nature Conservancy bought out most of the ranchers. Cattle numbers are being cut from about 10,000 to 200, and most of the park goes back to wilderness. Debate for the car: a win for nature, or the end of a working landscape?

Story time. On the 17th of June, 1579, the English captain Francis Drake sailed into a sheltered cove just over those hills. His ship, the Golden Hind, needed repairs after months of raiding Spanish towns and treasure ships up the Pacific coast, and he was about to sail home the long way, right round the world. He stayed about five weeks, and got on well with the Coast Mee-wok who lived here. He named the land New Albion, partly because its white cliffs reminded him of England, and claimed it for Queen Elizabeth the First, nailing up a brass plate with a sixpence showing her face. On the 23rd of July he sailed away, without leaving a colony. For centuries, people argued about exactly where he'd landed. Quiz: one of the best clues came from archaeologists, who found nearly a hundred pieces of something near the cove that had to have come from Drake. What? [[pause 6]] Chinese porcelain! Broken dishes that Drake had taken from a Spanish treasure ship and dumped here while lightening his ship for repairs. In 2021, California officially recognised Drake's Cove, inside the national seashore, as the site of New Albion.

Out on the Point Reyes peninsula is one of the wildest corners of California, and it's full of comeback stories. Quiz: when Europeans arrived, there were maybe half a million tule elk in California. By the 1870s, people thought they were extinct. How many were found, hiding in a marsh in the Central Valley? [[pause 5]] A single breeding pair! In 1978, ten tule elk were brought here to Toe-mah-less Point and fenced in. They thrived, then nearly half died in the drought of 2012 to 2015, and in 2020 activists illegally carried water to them. In December 2024, the Park Service finally breached the fence, and now they roam free. Then the elephant seals came back, starting a colony in 1981. During the government shutdown of January 2019, with no rangers around, they moved onto Drakes Beach and had their pups in the car park. And at the very tip is the Point Reyes Lighthouse, first lit in 1870, officially the windiest and foggiest spot on the Pacific coast. Unusually, it's built low, down about three hundred steps, to get the light below the fog.

Right now we're driving almost exactly along the San Andreas Fault. This straight valley is the fault zone. To the north it sinks under Toe-mah-less Bay; to the south it runs under Buh-lee-nus Lagoon. Then it heads out to sea and comes back on land near Daly City, which we'll pass this afternoon. Some numbers. The fault runs about 750 miles through California. The Pacific Plate, on your right, slides north about an inch a year compared with the North American Plate. But it doesn't slide smoothly. It sticks, builds up strain for decades, then lets go. In 1906, the ground along the fault shifted by up to twenty feet. After that earthquake, a Berkeley geology professor, Andrew Lawson, mapped all the fences and roads that had been sliced in half and shifted. They made an almost perfect line along a fault he'd found back in 1895. He named it after the San Andreas Valley, down the peninsula. We'll drive right past it near the airport. And the granite of Point Reyes, over there, matches the Sierra Nevada. It's been carried hundreds of miles north along this fault.

Somewhere across the lagoon is Buh-lee-nus, and you won't see a sign for it, because the locals keep tearing them down. Every road sign on Highway 1 pointing the way has been removed by residents. The county even put it to a vote, and the voters said: no more signs, thank you. It's a famously private little town of about fourteen hundred people. It also has a great property story. In 1927, an old dairy farm on the mesa was split into more than five thousand tiny lots, and a San Francisco newspaper sold many of them for 69 dollars and fifty cents each, as a subscription promotion. Buy the paper, get some land. Some of those streets have since fallen into the sea. And in March 2023, the town's post office closed, so the residents are petitioning to get it back. The water you're passing is Buh-lee-nus Lagoon, on the international list of important wetlands. The fault runs right down the middle of it, so Buh-lee-nus is on the Pacific Plate, creeping north away from Stinson Beach.

Stinson Beach! A long sandy beach that San Franciscans have been escaping to for 150 years. It started as Willow Camp, tents among the willows. After the 1906 earthquake, refugees from the city came out and opened some of its first businesses, and in 1916 it was renamed after the biggest landowners, Rose and Nathan Stinson. Sports fans: this is the finish line of the Dipsea, the oldest trail race in America. Since 1905, runners have raced seven and a half miles from Mill Valley, over the shoulder of Mount Tam, to this beach, with about 2,200 feet of climbing. You can take shortcuts with names like Suicide and the Swoop, and the oldest and youngest runners get up to a 25-minute head start. Quiz: so how young was the youngest-ever winner? [[pause 5]] Eight years old! Winners have been as old as 72. And Jack Kirk, the Dipsea Demon, finished 67 in a row and started his last one aged 96. One warning if you fancy a swim: these waters are in the Red Triangle, known for great white sharks.

The big mountain above us is Mount Tam-ul-pie-iss, Mount Tam to the locals, 2,571 feet at the East Peak. Myth-busting first. You'll hear that Tam-ul-pie-iss means Sleeping Maiden, from a Mee-wok legend about the mountain's profile. It doesn't. That legend was invented in Victorian times by a playwright, for a play at the mountain's outdoor theatre. The name really comes from the Coast Mee-wok tah-mal pah-heess, meaning west hill. From 1896 to 1930, a railway wound up from Mill Valley to the summit, with so many bends it was nicknamed the Crookedest Railroad in the World. And here's one for sports fans: this mountain is the birthplace of mountain biking. In the 1970s, riders bolted fat tyres and better brakes onto old 1930s and 40s Schwinn bikes and bombed down the fire roads. Their downhill races near Fairfax were called the Repack races, because the coaster brakes got so hot that the grease burned off, and riders had to repack their wheel bearings after every run. Gary Fisher, Charlie Kelly and Joe Breeze were among the pioneers.

Welcome to Muir Woods, one of the last old-growth redwood forests in the Bay Area, in a canyon on the side of Mount Tam that's wrapped in fog all summer. The redwoods drink that fog during the dry season. Here's how it survived. Mount Tam's redwoods were logged heavily to build San Francisco, and again to rebuild it after 1906. But the trees in this canyon were too hard to reach. In 1905, William Kent and his wife Elizabeth bought 611 acres of it for 45,000 dollars, with money borrowed from a banker friend. Then a water company tried to take part of it to build a dam and reservoir. So Kent used a brand-new law, the Antiquities Act, and offered the land to the nation. President Theodore Roosevelt accepted, and in January 1908 it became a national monument. The name first suggested was the Kent Monument, but Kent insisted on honouring the naturalist John Muir. The two later fell out, because Kent backed the dam that flooded Yosemite's Hetch Hetchy Valley. Kent went on to sponsor the law that created the National Park Service in 1916. He was also a loud supporter of anti-Asian immigration laws, so he's a complicated hero. The tallest tree here is 258 feet, most are 500 to 800 years old, and they grow from a seed the size of a tomato seed.

One more Muir Woods story. In April 1945, delegates from 50 countries gathered in San Francisco to write the Charter of the United Nations. President Franklin Roosevelt was due to open the conference, but he died on the 12th of April, just before it began. So on the 19th of May, the delegates came out here to Cathedral Grove and held a ceremony in his memory among the redwoods, and left a plaque in his honour. It's still there. And a practical note: Muir Woods gets up to six thousand visitors a day at peak times, and since 2018 you need a reservation to park or take the shuttle.

Five things about coast redwoods. One: they're the tallest living trees on Earth. The record holder, up in Humboldt County, is about 381 feet. Two: they can live about 2,000 years and grow 29 feet across. Three: they only grow in a narrow strip along the coast, from south of Big Sur up to the corner of Oregon, because they need fog. In dry summers they drink moisture straight out of the air. Four: before the Gold Rush they covered about two million acres. Today only about five percent of the old-growth forest is left. And five: the oldest, tallest trees tend to survive in deep, steep canyons, partly because loggers simply couldn't get them out. That's exactly how Muir Woods made it.

Welcome to Petaluma! Quiz: Petaluma's old nickname was the Egg Capital of the World, and it had a second nickname, a pun on the town's name. Any guesses? [[pause 5]] Chickaluma! This town was all about chickens. It had the only known poultry drugstore, a chemist's for chickens, and in 1879 Lyman Byce invented the coal-lamp egg incubator here. They still hold a Butter and Eggs Day parade. The land was part of Rancho Peh-tuh-loo-muh, granted in 1834 to our old friend General Vuh-lay-oh from Sonoma. In 1836 he built a huge adobe ranch house just east of town, the largest privately owned adobe ever built in California. And a lucky break: in 1906, Petaluma was barely damaged, thanks to solid bedrock, so it became the base for rescue and relief across the county. That's also why downtown still has its old iron-fronted buildings and Victorian houses.

We're passing San Rafael, the county seat of Marin. So who was Marin? The Coast Mee-wok have lived here for about 6,500 years, and more than 600 of their village sites have been found. According to General Vuh-lay-oh, who chaired the committee that named California's counties in 1850, this one was named after Marin, a great Coast Mee-wok chief. His birth name was Weak-moo-say. He was baptised Marino around the age of twenty, in 1801, and lived for years at Mission Dolores in San Francisco. Vuh-lay-oh believed he'd fought fierce battles against the Spanish. There's a rival theory: in 1775 the Spanish named the bay here after Our Lady of the Rosary, la Marinera, and Marin might just be short for that. I'm sticking with the chief. And a movie footnote: before it moved to the Preh-sid-ee-oh in San Francisco, George Lucas's company Lucasfilm had its headquarters here in San Rafael.

Skiers, this one's for you. If you live in San Francisco, your nearest big mountains are around Lake Tahoe. And the biggest ski resort there has quite a story. In 1956, Squaw Valley had one chairlift, two rope tows and a fifty-room lodge. And yet it won the right to host the 1960 Winter Olympics. Its founder, Alexander Cushing, sold it as a blank canvas, and California poured in money for roads, bridges, water and power. At the 1956 Games, there wasn't even a mayor to hand the Olympic flag to, because Squaw Valley wasn't a town. The 1960 Games were the first Winter Olympics televised live, with CBS paying just 50,000 dollars for the U.S. rights. It's also the only Winter Olympics with no bobsled, because the organisers decided a bobsled run wasn't worth building for the nine countries planning to enter. Today it's the biggest ski area around Lake Tahoe, joined to Alpine Meadows by a gondola. And in 2021 it changed its name to Palisades Tahoe, because the word squaw is a slur. Debate for the car: best ski resort any of you has ever skied. Go.

This junction, where Highway 1 meets 101, sits at the edge of Mill Valley, the town tucked into the redwood canyons on Mount Tam. People have lived here a very long time. Fourteen Coast Mee-wok village sites have been found around Mill Valley, with huge shell mounds along Richardson Bay. One, dug up in 1907, was twenty feet high. A plaque in a Mill Valley pavement marks the spot believed to be Chief Marin's birthplace, in 1781. And right around this intersection, in 1916, a roadhouse called the Blind Pig was built just outside the town limits, where the dry laws weren't enforced as strictly. During Prohibition, the roadhouses around here were known as gin joints, and worse.

Down to the left is Saw-suh-lee-toe, on Richardson Bay. The name is Spanish for little willow grove, and it's been spelled about a dozen ways over the years. Before the bridge, Saw-suh-lee-toe was the end of the line. Trains from up north, including that North Pacific Coast Railroad from the Russian River, met the ferries here. The car ferry to San Francisco took about twenty minutes and cost a dollar a car. In World War Two it became a shipbuilding town, and afterwards it went arty and wealthy, and famous for its houseboats. Quiz: when Saw-suh-lee-toe was laid out, planners assumed it would grow by filling in the bay, like San Francisco did. So what's odd about some of its streets? [[pause 5]] They're underwater! Streets with names like Pescadero, Eureka and Teutonia were mapped out, but they're still under Richardson Bay. More than a fifth of the city is water.

Those wild green hills on the right are the Marin Headlands. They look untouched, but they came close to becoming a city. In the 1960s, the government sold more than 2,000 acres here to a developer who planned a new town called Mar-in-chello, for 30,000 people, in 50 apartment towers, with housing estates, a shopping centre and a hotel. In 1970 the developer lost a lawsuit, and the land went to the Golden Gate National Recreation Area instead. The hills are also full of old forts and gun batteries from the 1890s to World War Two, built to keep enemy ships out of the bay, plus a Cold War Nike missile site. And every autumn, tens of thousands of hawks, falcons and eagles funnel down the peninsula over Hawk Hill, because they hate flying over open water.

Here it is, everyone! The Golden Gate Bridge! Cameras out, passengers. When it opened in 1937, it was the longest and tallest suspension bridge in the world: towers 746 feet tall, a main span of 4,200 feet. Plenty of experts said it couldn't be built at all, because of the wind, the fog and the tides. Quiz: the colour is International Orange, chosen by the architect Irving Morrow. But the U.S. Navy wanted something more visible to ships. What did they suggest? [[pause 5]] Black and yellow stripes! A giant bumblebee. Thank goodness for Morrow. Some infrastructure numbers for the engineers in the car. The two main cables contain about 80,000 miles of steel wire, more than three times round the Earth. Each tower has about 600,000 rivets. And the chief engineer, Joseph Strauss, insisted on safety nets under the workers. Nineteen men survived falls into them and formed the Half Way to Hell Club. Sadly, eleven men still died, ten in a single accident in February 1937.

Now the economics. After the 1929 crash, the bridge district couldn't sell its 30-million-dollar bond issue. Then in 1932, Amadeo Jah-nee-nee, founder of Bank of America, agreed to buy the whole lot to help the local economy. And the bonds were paid off in 1971, entirely from tolls. Those tolls, charged on the southbound side only, are still the district's main income, and that had a big side effect. In the 1950s and 60s, the district opposed running BART trains across the bridge, because it didn't want to lose toll money. That helped push Marin County out of the BART system altogether. So the reason there's no train from Marin to the city is basically a toll booth. One more for the road: for the bridge's 50th birthday in 1987, they let pedestrians on, and around 300,000 people packed the deck at once. The arch in the middle flattened out under their weight. Engineers say it was designed to flex, but they haven't tried it again.

Off the end of the bridge we're driving through the Preh-sid-ee-oh, a military base for 219 years. The Spanish founded it in 1776, the same year as the American Declaration of Independence, then it passed to Mexico, then to the U.S. Army in 1848, and in 1994 to the National Park Service. Lucasfilm now has its headquarters here. And the road you're on, the Preh-sid-ee-oh Parkway, replaced an old viaduct that wasn't safe in an earthquake. It cost 1.1 billion dollars, and the tunnels have a 14-acre park on their roof called Preh-sid-ee-oh Tunnel Tops. Down on the water is where the 2013 America's Cup was raced, in giant foiling catamarans that averaged about 30 knots and topped 40, as much as twice the speed of the wind. Quiz, sports fans: in a first to nine wins, Emirates Team New Zealand led Oracle Team USA 8 to 1. What happened next? [[pause 5]] Oracle won eight races in a row and kept the Cup! One of the greatest comebacks in sport, right there in the bay.

Nineteenth Avenue runs right through Golden Gate Park: 1,017 acres and about 24 million visitors a year. It was built from the 1870s on the Outside Lands, and three-quarters of it was sand dunes. Engineer William Hammond Hall and gardener John McLaren spent years planting grass and trees to hold the sand in place. At the ocean end there are two Dutch-style windmills from 1903 that used to pump water around the park. And this is where one of the world's weirdest races finishes. Bay to Breakers started on New Year's Day 1912, to show the rest of the country, buried in snow, that San Francisco was sunny. It runs 7.46 miles from near the bay to the breakers on Ocean Beach, finishing at the Great Highway, just past this park. People run it in fancy dress. In 1986 it set a Guinness world record as the biggest footrace on Earth, with 110,000 runners. Fancy-dress ideas for the three of you, if you ever enter, are welcome.

Welcome to San Francisco, Julia's home turf. A bit of its story, by the numbers. 1847: the town was a little trading post called Yerba Buena, with about 459 people. That January, its American mayor renamed it San Francisco, partly because General Vuh-lay-oh was planning a town called Francisca after his wife. San Francisco grabbed the name, so Vuh-lay-oh's town became Benicia. 1848 to 1849: the Gold Rush. From about 1,000 people to 25,000 in under two years. Ships' crews deserted to go dig for gold, leaving around 500 empty ships in the harbour. Some became warehouses, saloons and hotels, and some were deliberately sunk to claim the underwater land. Then the cove was filled in, so parts of downtown sit on top of Gold Rush ships. 1873: the first cable cars climb Clay Street. And 2024: San Francisco's economy was worth 268 billion dollars, about 324,000 dollars per person. That's the highest per-capita output of any big American city. Adam, there's your economics stat of the day.

Mike, this one's for you. You're driving through the home turf of your biggest rivals. In January 2013, four Stanford students launched a site called PaloAltoDelivery.com, down the Peninsula in Palo Alto. That summer, the startup accelerator Y Combinator gave them 120,000 dollars for seven percent of the company, and they renamed it DoorDash. Today DoorDash has 56 percent of the American food delivery market, it entered the Fortune 500 in 2024, and through Deliveroo and Volt it now operates all over Europe, including, of course, the UK. Meanwhile, from your side of the Atlantic: in 2020, Just Eat Takeaway agreed to buy Grubhub, one of DoorDash's American rivals, in a deal valuing it at 7.3 billion dollars. In November 2024 it sold Grubhub to Wonder Group for 650 million dollars. And in October 2025, Just Eat Takeaway itself was bought by the investment firm Pro-sus. I won't ask you to comment on that while driving. But the floor is open: who wins the delivery wars?

Story time: the morning San Francisco fell down. At 5:12 a.m. on the 18th of April, 1906, the San Andreas Fault ruptured along about 280 miles of coast, the same fault we followed past Toe-mah-less Bay and Buh-lee-nus this morning. A foreshock first, then about 42 seconds of violent shaking. Magnitude about 7.9. Then came the fires, burning for days. More than 3,000 people died, the deadliest earthquake in American history, and over 80 percent of the city was destroyed. At the time, San Francisco was the biggest city on the West Coast. Remember all the places it touched today: refugees opening businesses in Stinson Beach, Petaluma becoming the relief base, redwoods logged to rebuild the city. And the epicenter is now thought to have been just offshore from Mussel Rock, by Daly City, which is coming up next.

We're crossing into Daly City. After the 1906 earthquake, thousands of homeless San Franciscans headed south to the ranches here, including one belonging to John Daly, a dairyman who had married his boss's daughter. The town grew out of those refugees and took his name. From the late 1940s, developer Henry Dole-ger built Westlake, one of the first big planned suburbs, with rows and rows of near-identical houses up the hills. It inspired Malvina Reynolds' 1962 folk song Little Boxes, which pokes fun at exactly that. And a sadder side: Filipino American families who wanted to buy here in the 1950s were barred from Westlake by racial covenants, so they bought homes east of Hoo-nee-peh-roe Serra Boulevard instead.

Here's the strangest town of the whole trip: Colma. Most of its land is cemeteries. In 1900, San Francisco banned new burials in the city, and in 1912 it evicted most of its existing cemeteries. About 150,000 bodies were dug up and moved down here, at ten dollars per grave. Nearly everyone famous who died in San Francisco ended up here. Quiz: the dead here outnumber the living. By roughly how much? [[pause 5]] About a thousand to one! There are around one and a half million people buried in Colma. It's been called the City of the Silent, and its unofficial motto is: It's great to be alive in Colma.

Off to the right, just south of here, is San Andreas Lake, the lake in the valley that gave the San Andreas Fault its name. The fault runs straight down it, and its earth dam, built in 1868, sits right on top of the fault. It survived 1906. It's also part of one of the great feats of American water engineering. Julia, your tap water in San Francisco comes from Yosemite. The Hetch Hetchy Valley was dammed under a law passed in 1913, the Raker Act, after a huge political fight. John Muir was against it, and William Kent of Muir Woods supported it, which ended their friendship. Today, the Hetch Hetchy system sends water 167 miles across the Central Valley, and supplies 80 percent of the water for 2.6 million people. And the water is so clean, from bare Sierra granite, that San Francisco is one of only six American cities not required by law to filter its tap water. The dam also makes hydropower, which the city sold to PG&E, leading to decades of legal battles.

On the hills to the west is Sweeney Ridge, where Europeans first laid eyes on San Francisco Bay. In 1769, a Spanish expedition under Gaspar de Portolá was heading up the coast. Portolá sent scouts under Sergeant José Ortega north to find the Point Reyes headlands, which we drove past this morning. Ortega came back and said he couldn't get there, because the Golden Gate was in the way. And from Sweeney Ridge, on the 4th of November 1769, the expedition saw San Francisco Bay, although the scouts had spotted it a few days before. Think about that. Drake in 1579 and Viz-kuh-ee-no in 1603 sailed right past one of the greatest harbours on Earth and never noticed it, hidden behind the fog.

And here we are: San Francisco International. Last quiz of the trip: when the city opened its airport here in May 1927, what was the land being used for? [[pause 4]] It was a cow pasture! 150 acres, leased from the Mills family as a temporary, experimental airfield called Mills Field. The city bought it in 1931, and the word International was added after World War Two. Funny detail: it's owned by San Francisco, but it's actually in San Mateo County. So, Mike, Adam, Julia: that's a wrap! From the Gold Rush and Napa's vineyards to the Russian River, the Sonoma Coast, Point Reyes, the redwoods and the Golden Gate. Earthquakes, fusion, floating wind, delivery wars, and a town where the dead outnumber the living. It's been an honour being your guide. Safe flight, come back soon, and remember: Goonies never say die!
